scope.start: 20b: Rami bar Avin's identification of *itran* and *sha'avah* (21a opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 21b: Rav Kahana's statement on the height of the Hanukkah lamp (continues on 22a)

sections.title: The Mishnah's Unfit Materials: Terms, Bonfires, Kik Oil and Why They Fail
sections.gist: Notes on the Mishnah's list: what *itran* and *sha'avah* are, where the ban applies (a lamp, not a bonfire), three identifications of *shemen kik*, and Rabbah's two reasons for the ban.

children.title: Itran and Sha'avah as By-products: Why It Matters in Buying and Selling
children.gist: Rami bar Avin defines tar and wax as by-products of pitch and honey, and the Gemara finds the practical point in commerce.

bullets.text: Rami bar Avin: *itran* (tar) is the by-product of *zefet* (pitch), and *sha'avah* (wax) is the by-product of honey.
What difference does it make? Buying and selling: one who buys *itran* can insist on the by-product of pitch and nothing else, and the same holds for wax.
The definition confirms that the Mishnah's *sha'avah* is beeswax, and it has a direct use in commercial law, since it fixes what a seller must deliver.

children.title: Bonfire Yes, Lamp Wick No: The Scope of the Ban
children.gist: A Tosefta limits the ban on these materials to wicks for an oil lamp; a bonfire made of them is permitted, for heat or for light.

bullets.text: Tosefta: all the materials one may not light with on Shabbat may be used from the outset for a *medurah* (bonfire), to warm oneself or to use its light, on the ground or on a stove.
The Sages forbade them only as a wick for an oil lamp.
The concern is the mechanics of oil drawn up through a wick. Anyone who has lit oil lamps knows how finicky that is, and it is there that the quality of oil and wick matters.

children.title: Shemen Kik: A Sea Bird, Cotton Oil, or the Kikayon's Seeds?
children.gist: Three identifications of the Mishnah's *kik* oil, and Rabbah bar bar Chana's description of the *kikayon* plant.

bullets.text: Shmuel asked all the seafarers: there is a bird called *kik* in the coastal cities, and the oil comes from it.
Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda: it is cotton oil.
Reish Lakish: oil from the seed of a plant like Yonah's *kikayon*.

Rabbah bar bar Chana saw the species: like the ricinus tree, it grows in swamps and is set at shop entrances for shade. Oil is made from its seeds, and the sick of the West (Eretz Yisrael) rest under its branches.
Rashi: a plant of that species, not the very plant Yonah sat under. The Steinsaltz edition identifies it as the castor plant, and the medicinal use fits castor oil.

children.title: Rabbah's Reasons: Wicks Flicker, Oils Aren't Drawn
children.gist: Rabbah explains both halves of the Mishnah: unfit wicks make the flame flicker, and unfit oils are not drawn up by the wick.

bullets.text: Wicks: *mipnei she'ha'or mesakhsekhet bahen*, the flame sputters on them and doesn't burn well.
Oils: *mipnei she'einan nimshakhin achar ha'petilah*, they are not drawn up effectively by the wick.
Either way the lamp burns poorly, and one is likely to come and adjust it on Shabbat.

sections.title: Mixing Fit and Unfit: Added Oil, a Wrapped Wick, Molten Fat
sections.gist: Three test cases of combining fit and unfit material: Abaye's question on adding oil, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's nut, and Rav's ruling on molten fat, which turns on *gezeirah le'gezeirah*.

chart.caption: Combining fit and unfit materials: rulings and reasons
rows: Unfit oil with some fit oil added (Abaye's question)
The unfit oil may not be lit, so the mixture is forbidden too, lest one light it alone
Fit wick wrapped around unfit material, to light both
The unfit material burns as part of the wick
Fit wick wrapped around a nut, only to float it
The nut isn't lit; it only keeps the wick afloat
Molten fat or dissolved fish innards with some oil added (Rav)
Drawn by the wick in any case; their ban is only a decree, and no decree is added upon it

children.title: Abaye's Question: Fit Oil Added to Unfit Oil — A Decree?
children.gist: Abaye asks whether a little permitted oil makes an unfit oil usable; Rabbah forbids it, "because one may not light".

bullets.text: Abaye asks Rabbah: may one add any amount of permitted oil to the unfit oils and light? Do we decree lest one come to light the unfit oils alone, or not?
Rabbah: one may not light the mixture, "because one may not light".

The answer sounds circular. Rashi reads it as *lo plug*: since the oils are forbidden alone, the Sages make no distinction for the mixture. A variant reading, *lefi she'einan nidlakin*, is a factual claim: even mixed, they don't burn well.
R. Akiva Eiger (Gilyon HaShas) notes similar self-referential phrasing, even in the Torah: a blemished kohen "shall not approach... for any man who has a blemish shall not approach" (Vayikra 21).

The whole discussion is rabbinic. No mitzvah of lighting a Shabbat lamp has been introduced yet, only the worry, as with reading by lamplight and food on the fire, that one will tamper with the flame.

children.title: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's Nut: Lighting Together or Only Floating?
children.gist: Abaye challenges Rabbah from a wick wrapped around a nut; the Gemara prefers that challenge as *ma'aseh rav*, answers that the nut only floated the wick, and reads the whole Tosefta as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's.

bullets.text: Abaye objects from a Tosefta: a fit material wrapped around an unfit one may not be lit. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: in my father's house they wrapped a wick around a nut and lit it. So combining fit and unfit is permitted.
Rabbah: before you challenge me from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, support me from the first *tanna*, who forbids it.
The Gemara: it is better to challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's testimony, because *ma'aseh rav*: a practical precedent carries more weight than a stated ruling.

How heavily a *ma'aseh rav* weighs against the first *tanna* remains a real question. A precedent of leniency may say more about normative practice than a personal stringency, like Rabban Gamliel's white garment for the kohen in the previous chapter, which is not followed.
Answer: the nut wasn't lit together with the wick; it served *le'hakpot*, to float the wick on the oil.

Then why does the first *tanna* forbid it? The whole Tosefta is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's and is incomplete (*chasurei mechsera*): wrapping in order to light both together is forbidden; using the unfit material only to float the wick is permitted, as in his father's house.
This is the floating wick familiar from Hanukkah lamps, with the nut as the float.

children.title: Molten Fat and Fish Innards: No Gezeirah upon a Gezeirah
children.gist: Rav permits molten fat with a little oil added; Rabbah distinguishes materials that are drawn by the wick and banned only by decree, and the Gemara declines to add a decree upon a decree.

bullets.text: So far: a mixture of permitted and unfit oil may not be lit. But Rav Beruna citing Rav: molten fat, or fish innards that dissolved, may be lit once any amount of oil is added.

Rabbah: these are drawn by the wick even in their natural state, and the unfit oils are not. Molten fat was banned only because of unmolten fat, and dissolved innards because of undissolved ones; the Sages didn't extend that decree to a mixture with oil.
Why not decree against the mixture because of molten fat without oil? That ban is itself a decree, and one does not add a decree upon a decree (*gezeirah le'gezeirah*).
The principle isn't absolute; elsewhere the Gemara does sometimes layer decrees, but here it declines.
Tosafot asks: isn't the whole ban on unfit wicks and oils already a fence around the fear of adjusting the lamp, so that banning a mixture is already a second layer?

The Rivan (in Tosafot) gives another reason for avoiding such oils: not *shema yateh*, that one will adjust the lamp, but *shema yikhbeh*, that it will go out and leave the house dark, harming *shalom bayit*. This treats the Shabbat lamp as a mitzvah in its own right.

Tosafot records a tradition that one fit lamp in the house lets other rooms use unfit wicks and oils, which may not fit the stated reason; and a second answer, that unfit lamps may serve activities one could do in the dark, since there is no reason to adjust them.

sections.title: The Temple Menorah: Same Standard, and Worn Priestly Garments as Wicks
sections.gist: Rami bar Chama applies the Shabbat standard to the Menorah from *leha'alot ner tamid*; two sources about priestly garments turned into wicks are then reconciled with it.

children.title: Leha'alot Ner Tamid: A Flame That Rises of Itself
children.gist: Wicks and oils unfit for Shabbat are unfit for the Menorah too, since its flame must rise on its own.

bullets.text: Rami bar Chama's baraita: wicks and oils unfit for Shabbat may not be lit in the Temple either, from Shemot 27:20, "*leha'alot ner tamid*".
His explanation: the flame must rise by itself once kindled, not by means of something else, such as adjusting the wick.
Rashi reads the causative verb: you make the flame ascend, and then it must sustain itself (*shalhevet olah me'eleha*), the same self-sufficiency required on Shabbat.

children.title: Worn Priestly Garments as Wicks: Beit HaSho'evah Lanterns, and Linen Only
children.gist: Two sources seem to use wool-containing priestly garments as wicks; the first concerns the Beit HaSho'evah lanterns, not the Menorah, and the second only linen garments.

bullets.text: Challenge from a Mishnah: the kohanim's worn trousers and belts were unraveled into wicks, lit at the *Simchat Beit HaSho'evah*. The belts contained wool (*tekhelet*), which is unfit.
Answer: the *Simchat Beit HaSho'evah* is different. The Menorah wasn't lit there, only special lanterns, and they weren't particular about those wicks.
Challenge from Rabbah bar Mattana: worn priestly garments were unraveled into wicks for the Temple. Doesn't that include garments of *kilayim*, like the wool-and-linen belt?
Answer: no, those wicks were made only from linen garments.
Linen is a fit wick material, so wicks from the linen garments meet the Menorah's standard.

sections.title: Unfit Wicks and Oils on Hanukkah: Relighting and Using the Light
sections.gist: Rav Huna, Rav Chisda and Rav differ according to two premises, whether a lamp that goes out must be relit (*kavtah zakuk lah*) and whether its light may be used; then a challenge from "sunset until traffic ceases".

children.title: Forbidden Always, Weekdays Only, or Never: Rav Huna, Rav Chisda, Rav
children.gist: Each position follows from its two premises on relighting and on using the light; Abaye's hesitant acceptance of Rav's reasoning is recorded.

bullets.text: Rav Huna: wicks and oils unfit for Shabbat are forbidden for Hanukkah, on Shabbat and on weekdays alike.
Rava explains: he holds *kavtah zakuk lah*, so one must use materials that burn well from the start; and using the light is permitted on weekdays, so on Shabbat one might come to adjust it.
Rav Chisda: permitted on weekdays, forbidden on Shabbat. He holds *kavtah ein zakuk lah*, but also that using its light is permitted, so on Shabbat one might adjust the flame in order to use it.
R. Zeira citing Rav Mattana (others: R. Zeira citing Rav): permitted for Hanukkah, on weekdays and on Shabbat alike.
R. Yirmeya explains: Rav holds *kavtah ein zakuk lah* and *asur le'hishtamesh le'orah*, so even on Shabbat there is no fear of adjusting the wick.
For Rav Chisda what counts is the lamp's capacity at the moment of lighting: enough oil and a sheltered place fulfill the mitzvah even if it later goes out.

The halakha follows *kavtah ein zakuk lah*. A practical question: lighting outdoors in the wind with the lantern's glass doors open. If at the moment of lighting the flame had no real chance to last, some question whether the mitzvah was done even if the doors are then closed.

chart.caption: Unfit wicks and oils for Hanukkah: three views and their premises
rows: Rav (per R. Zeira; explained by R. Yirmeya)

children.title: Abaye and Girsa De'yankuta: Why It Matters Whom One Hears First
children.gist: Abaye rejected Rav's reasoning in R. Yirmeya's name but accepted it in R. Yochanan's, and regretted not learning it from the start, since learning in youth lasts.

bullets.text: The Sages told this halakha to Abaye in R. Yirmeya's name and he didn't accept it. When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael and said it in R. Yochanan's name, he accepted it.
Abaye: had I merited, I would have learned it from the outset.
What difference does it make, since he learned it in the end? *Girsa de'yankuta*: what is learned in youth is better remembered.
The Gemara treats early learning as better for retention, not as mere sentiment.

children.title: "From Sunset Until Traffic Ceases": Duration, Window or Measure?
children.gist: A baraita seems to require the lamp to burn until the market empties; the Gemara reads it as the window for lighting, or as the amount of oil required.

bullets.text: Challenge to *kavtah ein zakuk lah*: a baraita says the mitzvah runs from sunset *ad she'tikhleh regel min ha'shuk*. Doesn't that mean one must relight so it burns the whole time?
No: it means that one who hasn't lit at sunset may still light until traffic ceases.
Alternatively, it gives the measure: the lamp needs oil and wick enough for that period. If it then goes out early, one need not relight.
Whether the window opens at sunset or at *tzeit ha'kokhavim* is debated among the rishonim.

returns_to.note: Tests *kavtah ein zakuk lah*, held by Rav Chisda and Rav

children.title: Until When? When the Tarmoda'ei Leave the Market
children.gist: R. Yochanan: traffic ceases when the wood-sellers from Tadmor, the last in the market, go home.

bullets.text: Rabbah bar bar Chana citing R. Yochanan: until the traffic of the *Tarmoda'ei* ceases.
They sold kindling wood and stayed latest, for people who found at nightfall that they had run out.
Rashi describes them as non-Jewish vendors, which answers when Jews could see the lights while they themselves were busy lighting.

The Shulchan Aruch sets the time at about half an hour, reflecting his place and time; the standard is really local. A Jerusalem rabbi kept his lamp burning until midnight because he lived opposite a cinema whose last showing ended then.
Once lighting moved indoors under danger, the audience became the household and timing became more lenient. Today many place the lamp in a window facing out, which is to be encouraged.

sections.title: Kindling the Hanukkah Lights: How Many, Where, and a Light to Use
sections.gist: The levels of observance with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's dispute and its reasons, where the lamp is placed, and Rava's rule of a second light for use.

children.title: Ner Ish U'veito, Mehadrin, Mehadrin Min Ha'mehadrin: Eight Down or One Up
children.gist: The basic mitzvah is one light per household; the *mehadrin* light one per person; the *mehadrin min ha'mehadrin* change the number nightly, down from eight for Beit Shammai and up from one for Beit Hillel.

bullets.text: Baraita: the basic mitzvah is *ner ish u'veito*, one light each night for the head of the household and his household.
The *mehadrin* light one for each member of the household.
The *mehadrin min ha'mehadrin* change the number each night. Beit Shammai: eight on the first night, decreasing to one. Beit Hillel: one on the first night, increasing to eight.
*Mehadrin* comes from *hadar*: beautifying a mitzvah, not stringency, unlike its modern use for strict kashrut supervision.

Rishonim differ at the top level. Tosafot: the household returns to one set of lights, since several people lighting different numbers would hide which night it is. Rambam: each person keeps lighting, with the night's number. Ashkenazi practice follows the Rambam here, unusually.

illustration.caption: The *mehadrin min ha'mehadrin* night by night: Beit Shammai light eight on the first night and one fewer each night, and Beit Hillel light one and add one each night, with the reasons given on 21b.

children.title: Why Down or Up? Days to Come or Past, Festival Bulls or Ma'alin Ba'kodesh
children.gist: Two amora'im in Eretz Yisrael explain the dispute differently, and two elders in Sidon practiced each way, citing the second pair of reasons.

bullets.text: Ulla: two amora'im in the West, R. Yosei bar Avin and R. Yosei bar Zevida, disagree about the reasons.
One: Beit Shammai count the incoming days, those still to come; Beit Hillel count the outgoing days, those already observed.

The other: Beit Shammai follow the Festival bulls of Sukkot, thirteen on the first day and one fewer each day after (Bamidbar 29). Beit Hillel follow *ma'alin ba'kodesh ve'ein moridin*: in holiness one rises and does not descend.
Rabbah bar bar Chana citing R. Yochanan: two elders in Sidon, one following Beit Shammai because of the Festival bulls, the other Beit Hillel because of *ma'alin ba'kodesh*.
Maharal: counting down from eight looks to potential, the days yet to come; counting up looks to what is actual, the night one is in.
A simpler image: counting down is a countdown to the end, counting up an openness to growing joy.

Rav Shlomo Zevin: the question is whether Hanukkah is about removing evil or spreading good. The declining bulls stand for the nations diminishing; *ma'alin ba'kodesh* for holiness spreading. Fire destroys evil; light spreads good.

The Festival bulls: 13 on the first day, one fewer each day
One elder practiced so, citing the Festival bulls

children.title: Placement: Outside the Entrance, the Window, or the Table in Danger
children.gist: The lamp goes outside the entrance so all can see it; upstairs, at the window by the public domain; in a time of danger, on one's table.

bullets.text: Baraita: the mitzvah is to place the Hanukkah lamp at the entrance to one's house, on the outside, so that all can see it.
One who lives upstairs places it at the window adjacent to the public domain.
In a time of danger, when gentiles decreed against kindling lights, one places it on his table, and that suffices.
Rashi: the entrance is the one to the courtyard, so those coming and going see it in the doorframe. The danger was a Persian (Zoroastrian) decree that fire be kindled only at their temples.
The move indoors shifted the publicizing of the miracle from passers-by to the household, as the Shulchan Aruch rules. With religious freedom today, the common practice is a window facing out.

children.title: A Second Light for Use: Rava, the Bonfire and the Important Person
children.gist: Since the Hanukkah lights may not be used, Rava requires another light for use, unless a bonfire is burning, and even then for an important person.

bullets.text: Rava: one needs another light in order to use its light, since one may not use the Hanukkah lights.
If a bonfire is burning, no extra light is needed; one can use the bonfire's light.
An important person, who doesn't use a bonfire's light, needs another light even when a bonfire is burning.
This is the source of the *shamash*. Rashi stresses a second purpose: the extra light shows onlookers that the Hanukkah lights aren't there for illumination.
An important person uses refined lamplight, not a torch, so only a separate lamp shows that the Hanukkah lights serve another purpose. Today electric light plays the role of the bonfire.

returns_to.note: Assumes Rav's view that the Hanukkah light may not be used

sections.title: What Is Hanukkah? Megillat Ta'anit, the Defiled Oils and the Sealed Cruse
sections.gist: The Gemara's account of the holiday: eight days from the 25th of Kislev, the one sealed cruse that burned eight days, and the Sages' institution of *hallel* and thanksgiving.

bullets.text: "What is Hanukkah?" A baraita from *Megillat Ta'anit*: from the 25th of Kislev, the days of Hanukkah are eight, on which one may not eulogize or fast.
When the Greeks entered the *Heikhal* they defiled all its oils. When the Hasmonean kingdom defeated them, they searched and found only one cruse, lying under the seal of the *Kohen Gadol*.
It had oil to light for only one day; a miracle occurred and they lit from it for eight days.
The next year the Sages fixed these days as festive days, with *hallel* and thanksgiving (*hoda'ah*).
*Megillat Ta'anit* is among the earliest rabbinic works, a list of days barred for fasting and eulogy, mostly for forgotten events. The story here comes from a Babylonian gloss on it.
Rashi: not a *Yom Tov* that bars *melakhah*, but *hallel* and *al ha'nissim*. Lighting itself is not named among what was instituted.
The Beit Yosef's question: there was oil for one day, so the miracle was only seven days. Maharal: each night only an eighth of the oil burned, so the miracle appeared all eight days.

Sources from the period and from Eretz Yisrael (Maccabees, Josephus, *al ha'nissim*) speak of the victory and rededication, not the oil. Maharal: the small miracle revealed the divine hand in the victory, so the oil and the war are interlocking, not competing, stories.
The graded levels up to *mehadrin min ha'mehadrin* may mirror a miracle that itself went beyond what was needed.

sections.title: The Hanukkah Lamp's Height: Ten Handbreadths, Twenty Cubits
sections.gist: A Mishnah on fire damage suggests the lamp belongs within ten handbreadths of the ground, though the proof is deflected; Rav Kahana then begins R. Tanchum's upper limit.

children.title: The Camel, the Flax and the Hanukkah Lamp: Proof for Ten Handbreadths?
children.gist: R. Yehuda exempts a storekeeper whose Hanukkah lamp outside set a passing camel's flax alight; Ravina infers the lamp belongs within ten handbreadths, but the exemption may only be to avoid burdening the mitzvah.

bullets.text: Mishnah (damages): a spark flies from under a hammer and causes damage outside the workshop; the one who struck is liable.

A camel laden with flax passes through the public domain, its flax enters a store and catches fire from the storekeeper's lamp: the camel owner is liable. If the storekeeper placed his lamp outside, the storekeeper is liable.
R. Yehuda: if it was a Hanukkah lamp placed outside the store's entrance, the storekeeper is exempt, since he was entitled to put it there.

Ravina citing Rabbah: this shows the mitzvah is to place the lamp within ten handbreadths of the ground. Otherwise the camel owner could say: you should have set it above the height of a camel and its rider.
Deflected: perhaps above ten handbreadths is also allowed, and R. Yehuda exempts the storekeeper so as not to burden the mitzvah, lest people refrain from lighting.

returns_to.note: The lamp placed outside the entrance, as the baraita requires

children.title: Rav Kahana in the Name of R. Tanchum: An Upper Limit
children.gist: Returning to the lamp's height, the Gemara opens Rav Kahana's statement, which continues on the next daf.

bullets.text: On the matter itself, Rav Kahana says that Rav Natan bar Manyumi taught in the name of R. Tanchum; the statement follows on the next daf.

children.continues: Continues on 22a: a Hanukkah lamp placed above twenty cubits is invalid, like a sukkah or an alleyway beam above twenty cubits, since people don't look up that high.

key_terms.sense: oil drawn up by the wick
key_terms.definition: Whether a lamp oil is drawn up steadily through the wick to feed the flame. An oil that isn't drawn well makes the lamp burn poorly.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rabbah gives it as the reason certain oils are unfit for the Shabbat lamp, and it separates molten fat, which is drawn, from the truly unfit oils.

key_terms.sense: a decree to protect a decree
key_terms.definition: The principle that the Sages generally do not enact a protective decree whose only purpose is to safeguard another rabbinic decree.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Molten fat with oil added is permitted, because the ban on molten fat is itself a decree and no further decree is added to protect it.

key_terms.definition: The principle that a ruling shown by the actual practice of a great sage carries more weight than a stated theoretical ruling.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara prefers Abaye's challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's testimony about his father's house because it is a practical precedent.

key_terms.sense: obligation to relight a mitzvah lamp that went out
key_terms.definition: The question whether a lamp lit for a mitzvah that goes out must be rekindled, or whether the mitzvah was fulfilled at the lighting.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Huna holds one must relight, so Hanukkah wicks and oils must be reliable; Rav Chisda and Rav hold one need not, and a baraita about sunset to the market's emptying is read to fit that view.

key_terms.sense: personal use of a mitzvah lamp's light
key_terms.definition: Whether one may use the light of a lamp lit for a mitzvah, such as the Hanukkah lamp, for ordinary purposes like reading or working.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda permit using the Hanukkah light and so fear one will adjust it on Shabbat; Rav forbids it, and Rava requires a separate light for use.

key_terms.definition: Those who perform a mitzvah in a more beautiful or fuller way than its basic requirement; the mehadrin min ha'mehadrin go further still.
key_terms.on_this_daf: For Hanukkah the basic mitzvah is one light per household, the mehadrin light one per person, and the mehadrin min ha'mehadrin vary the number nightly.

key_terms.definition: The principle that matters of holiness are raised to a higher level and not lowered.
key_terms.on_this_daf: On one amora's view it is Beit Hillel's reason for adding a Hanukkah light each night, against Beit Shammai's model of the Festival bulls.

judgment_calls: The Hanukkah material (s13, s18, s23, s24) could sit under one umbrella section 'The Hanukkah Lights', and s1, s6, s10 under 'Unfit Wicks and Oils'; kept as separate top-level sections because each is a self-contained discussion and the umbrellas would push the key disputes a level deeper.

Rami bar Avin's definitions (s2) begin on 20b; grouped with the other notes on the Mishnah's list rather than given their own top-level section, since they share the purpose of explaining the Mishnah.
The Tarmoda'ei (s17) could be a sibling of the sunset-to-market challenge; nested under it because it explains the phrase that the challenge quotes.
Abaye's regret (s15) nested under the three Hanukkah positions because it concerns the transmission of Rav's reasoning; it could stand as a separate step.
The levels of observance (s19) hold the reasons for the dispute (s20) as a child; the reasons could be a sibling, but they only explain the baraita's dispute.
Rava's second light (s22) could be grouped with the three positions on using the light; kept with the kindling baraitot where it falls, with a returns_to link.

The flax case (s25) and Rav Kahana's opening line (s26) are grouped under the lamp's height, since the Gemara introduces Rav Kahana 'on the matter itself'; s26 could instead be a stub top-level section.
coverage_notes: The essay opens with a clarification of wax and paraffin candles (Tosafot, Shulchan Aruch), a return to the Mishnah's sha'avah on 20b.14; outside this daf's scope and left out.
20b.15–21a.1 (Rami bar Avin; buying and selling) is covered at the end of the previous shiur's essay; that material was used and the section is not flagged.
21b.11–21b.13 (the camel and flax Mishnah, R. Yehuda, Ravina's inference, the start of Rav Kahana's statement) is not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the Gemara text only.

The essay presents ma'aseh rav as Rabbah's response and suggests one could then mix fit and unfit oil; in the text Rabbah asks for support from the first tanna, the Gemara explains Abaye's preference for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as ma'aseh rav, and the conclusion stands that the mixture is forbidden. Followed the text.

The essay resolves the Tosefta as 'no debate' between the tanna kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; the text says the whole baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's and is incomplete. Followed the text.

The essay gives the priestly-garment answers in reverse order and as one challenge; the text has two challenges, first the Simchat Beit HaSho'evah lanterns (belts), then Rabbah bar Mattana's baraita (linen garments only). Followed the text.
The essay says Shmuel's bird is found in 'the islands of the sea'; the text says cities on the sea coast. Followed the text.
The essay says the kikayon was draped over shop doorways to attract customers; the text says it was placed there for shade. Followed the text.

The essay suggests kik and cotton oils are unfit because they make the flame flicker; in the text Rabbah attributes flickering to wicks and poor drawing to oils. Followed the text and omitted the claim.
